Notes: Year Established basis: Encyclopaedia Judaica (2007) states that after the division of Alexander's empire Ascalon came under Ptolemaic rule and 'A Jewish community flourished in the city under their rule' - earliest documented Jewish presence found. Ptolemaic rule over Palestine c. 301-200 BCE; midpoint -250 used (c.). No count given; an organized community is implied. Earlier context (not rows): Babylonian destruction 604 BCE; Persian-period Ashkelon was a Phoenician city under Tyre (Pseudo-Scylax); c. 242 BCE the Jewish tax-farmer Joseph son of Tobiah executed twenty Ascalonite notables (Josephus Ant. 12.4.5) - an official action not residence. Ashkelon kept its independence against the Hasmoneans (EJ).

Encyclopedia of the Bible (Zondervan, on Bible Gateway) states that when Jonathan the Maccabee came to Ascalon (1 Macc 10:86, c. 147 BCE; again 11:60) 'The large Jewish population appears to have sided with the Maccabees'. Claim of a large Jewish population is unquantified and not supported by other sources found (EJ says Ashkelon remained an independent Hellenistic city never conquered by the Hasmoneans); year c. -147 from 1 Macc 10:86.

Herod's sister Salome (of the Idumaean-Jewish Herodian family) resided in Ashkelon per the Jewish Encyclopedia (1906), citing Josephus; Augustus granted her the royal palace of Ascalon after Herod's death (Josephus War 2.6.3, c. 4 BCE). A single elite Jewish individual, not a community. Herod (by some traditions born in Ashkelon) built baths, fountains and colonnades there (War 1.21.11) though the city lay outside his kingdom.

Mishnah Eduyot 8:2: R. Yose the Priest and R. Zechariah ben HaKatzav (a priest active at the very end of the Second Temple period) testified about a young Jewish girl 'taken as collateral' (by gentiles) in Ashkelon, whom her family then distanced. Mishnah speaking of pre-70 conditions; date c. 60 CE (late Second Temple period, approximate). Attests individual Jews in Ashkelon; whether the family were residents is not stated.

Josephus War 2.18.5 (66 CE): after the Caesarea massacre and Jewish reprisal raids that attacked Askelon (War 2.18.1), 'the other cities rose up against the Jews that were among them; those of Askelon slew two thousand five hundred' and imprisoned others. 2500 is an ancient death toll of Jews living in (or around) Ascalon, not a population count - Population left blank; it implies a substantial resident Jewish community before the revolt. Later (War 3.2.1-3, winter 66/67) Jewish rebel forces attacking Ascalon - 'always an enemy to the Jews' - lost 10000 and then 8000 men; these are attackers' casualties, not residents. No source found stating that no Jews remained afterwards.
